changes.before: Give images useful descriptions and controls clear names. Check every action with the keyboard.
changes.after: Describe a useful picture and give a button a clear name.

before: Accessibility means making content and actions usable by people with different ways of seeing, hearing, moving, and understanding. Someone might use a keyboard, a screen reader, a touch screen, or a large zoom setting. Your HTML should still tell them what is there and what each control does. Start with built-in elements that already have useful behavior. A button is an action control; an a with href is a navigation link. Their meaning helps a browser and assistive tools offer the right interaction.

This is a complete example with an informative image and a named control. ```html Bike repair day

Bike repair day

``` The image requires a repair.jpg file. alt describes its useful information. The button has visible words that explain its purpose. This HTML creates the control; it does not yet supply code to open repair times.

An image's src tells the browser which picture to load. alt gives a text replacement. Imagine someone cannot see this picture: what information would they miss? Write that information in ordinary words. You usually do not need “picture of,” because the tool can already announce that it is an image. Decorative pictures that add no information normally have alt="". Do not leave alt out and assume that is the same: some tools may announce the file name. img has no closing tag because it is a void element, with no content inside it.

A control's accessible name is the name assistive tools use to identify it. For an ordinary button, its visible text supplies that name. Clear visible text helps everyone. Prefer “View repair times” to “Go” when the action would otherwise be unclear. type="button" makes it a plain button; inside a form, this avoids accidentally submitting the form. A native button can receive keyboard focus and can be activated using normal keyboard controls. A div with button-like styling does not automatically gain those behaviors.

This fragment belongs inside body and demonstrates navigation beside an action control. ```html Read directions to the workshop ``` The link needs a directions.html page and navigates to it. The button needs behavior added later if it should show a checklist. The small dot is decorative, so its empty alt lets assistive tools skip it. These choices depend on each element's purpose, not on its color or shape. Do not copy empty alt onto a picture that teaches useful information.

Keyboard focus marks the control that will receive a keyboard action. Press Tab to move forward through focusable controls and Shift+Tab to move backward. Check that you can see where focus is. A focused button should be usable with Enter or Space; a link normally activates with Enter. tabindex="-1" removes an element from normal Tab navigation, so it is not a way to make this exercise's button easy to reach. Keep the source order sensible and keep visible focus styling. These are useful checks, but they do not cover every accessibility need.

For the picnic exercise, add alt text that describes the informative image and give the native button the exact visible name View picnic details. Keep it keyboard focusable. Tab to it, check its name, and inspect focus. The automated checks verify text and basic focusability; the starter does not add the actual details-opening behavior. A button passing the naming check can still do nothing when activated. To judge a finished interactive page, test the real action, review images in context, and use a screen reader as well as the keyboard.
after: People use pages in different ways. Some use a mouse, some use a keyboard, and some use a screen reader that reads the page aloud. Clear HTML helps people understand the page and use its controls.

This example describes a picture and names a button. ```html ``` `src` gives the picture’s filename. `alt` gives words for someone who cannot see it. The button’s text says what it is for. The photo is a practice filename, not an included file. The button needs JavaScript later to perform its action.

`alt` is a text replacement for an image. Describe the useful information someone would miss without seeing it. For a real image, look at the image before writing the description. A purely decorative image can use `alt=""` so a screen reader can skip it.

A button’s visible words usually give it the name a screen reader announces. Use clear words such as `View repair times`. Keep `type="button"` for a button that should not submit a form. A real `<button>` already supports keyboard use.

Use a link to go somewhere and a button to do something. ```html Read workshop directions ``` The link points to another page. The button is for an action on the page. This small example names that action but does not yet add the code to do it.

Keyboard focus shows which control is ready for your next key press. Press Tab to move forward and Shift+Tab to move back. Make sure you can see the focused control. Enter activates a link. Enter or Space activates a button.

For this practice, imagine the picnic photo shows neighbors sharing food at a park table. Add an `alt` description of that scene. Name the button exactly `View picnic details` and set `type="button"`. The photo file is not included. This task checks the description and button name; it does not add the action that opens details.
